MofyAlly EDGE™ — Personalised Trading Intelligence Platform

The objective should be to build more than a trade journal. MofyAlly EDGE should become a trader's personal trading record, execution-monitoring system, risk manager, and performance intelligence platform, connecting the different platforms and brokers they use into one personalised workspace.

The core principle is simple: every trader should have one complete, trustworthy record of their trading activity, regardless of where they analyse, execute, manage, or close a trade.

For example, a trader might analyse Gold on TradingView, execute the trade through a connected broker, manage another account on MT5, and hold a separate funded account with a different broker. MofyAlly EDGE should bring these records together without confusing the accounts, duplicating trades, or losing the original execution details.

1. The complete trading journey

1. Personal trader profile

Trading goals, experience, strategy, risk tolerance, instruments, routines and account rules

2. Connect trading platforms and brokers

TradingView-connected brokers, MT5, other supported brokers and manual/import options

3. Capture every trading event

Orders, fills, position changes, stop-loss changes, partial closes, fees and final outcomes

4. Personal trade journal

Original thesis, screenshots, setup, confluence, emotions, execution and review

5. Risk and rule monitoring

Position risk, drawdown, exposure, daily loss limits and funded-account rules

6. Performance intelligence

Strategy statistics, recurring mistakes, execution quality, reviews and personalised improvement plans

The system must preserve the distinction between automatically recorded facts and the trader's own interpretation. For example, an executed price can be imported from the broker, but a claim that a trade was based on a liquidity sweep must come from a pre-trade record, a supported chart analysis, or an explicitly labelled post-trade observation.

2. Design the personalisation engine first

Personalisation should begin before the first trade is imported. Each trader needs a profile that shapes their journal, risk calculations, dashboards, reminders, and review questions.

Proposed onboarding fields for MofyAlly EDGE

A. Trader identity and goals

Experience level, trading goals, preferred trading hours, target habits, learning objectives and preferred review frequency.

B. Trading style and strategy

Scalping, intraday or swing trading; instruments; timeframes; setup definitions; entry triggers; invalidation criteria; and exit rules.

C. Accounts and broker rules

Broker, platform, account currency, demo/live/funded status, balance, leverage where available, commission and swap model, and any evaluation or payout rules.

D. Personal risk policy

Risk per trade, maximum daily loss, maximum open exposure, stop-trading conditions, and whether limits are personal targets or externally imposed rules.

E. Psychology and habits

Optional self-reported emotions, common mistakes, revenge-trading triggers, confidence, fatigue and post-trade reflection preferences.

Make the system adapt to the individual

For example, if a trader selects XAUUSD and a strategy based on liquidity sweeps, market structure shifts and fair value gaps, their trade form should prioritise those fields. A swing trader using a different strategy should see a different template.

The trader must be able to edit their profile, switch strategies, create custom fields and maintain different rules for each account. Personalisation should not silently change historical records when a strategy or risk setting changes.

3. Build a genuine multi-platform connection system

This is the most technically important part of your request. Do not build one generic connector and assume it will work with every trading platform. Build a common integration framework with separate, tested connectors.

The platform integration research and your existing blueprint support this approach: MT5 can expose account, position and history data through its terminal/Python integration, while TradingView has a distinct webhook alert mechanism and a separate formal process for broker trading integrations.

Connector 1 — MetaTrader 5 (MT5)

First priority

Create a read-only Expert Advisor (EA) or a supported terminal-side connector. Capture fills/deals, orders, open positions, history, SL/TP changes where observable, and account information. Include history backfill, reconnection, and reconciliation.

MT5 supports account and trading-history access through its Python integration; the connector must be tested against real broker-specific behaviour.

+1

Connector 2 — TradingView

Support TradingView alerts and webhook messages to record signals, setup events and chart context. Where a user executes through a broker connected to TradingView, capture the actual fill from that broker's supported account-data interface—not from an alert alone.

TradingView webhooks notify external services when configured alerts fire; they do not by themselves prove that an order filled.

TradingView

Connector 3 — Other brokers and platforms

For each broker, assess official APIs, OAuth access, transaction/history endpoints, streaming or polling options, permitted scopes and commercial access conditions. Build a dedicated connector only when the required data can be accessed reliably and lawfully.

Broker capabilities differ. For example, Webull documents a separate OAuth-based Connect API for authorised third-party integrations.

Webull API

Connector 4 — Universal fallback

Add CSV/Excel import, supported statement uploads and manual capture. This ensures traders can use the journal even when their broker has no API or direct connection is unavailable.

Critical distinction: TradingView alerts versus executed trades

The system must recognise three separate events:

  • Signal received: a TradingView alert or strategy event was generated.

  • Order submitted: an order was sent to a broker.

  • Execution confirmed: the broker reports an actual fill or deal.

These events must not be treated as interchangeable. A signal can fire without an order, and an order can be rejected, partially filled, cancelled or executed at a different price.

Also, being able to trade through a broker inside TradingView does not automatically mean a third-party journal can read that broker's account. Each integration must be assessed for actual account-data access, permissions and history coverage. If an official connection is not available, use a supported broker connector, an approved intermediary, an alert-only connection, or manual import—and label the resulting coverage honestly.

4. Create a universal trade-event engine

Every connector should translate its incoming data into one common internal format. This is how MofyAlly EDGE can compare trades across different platforms without treating their records as identical.

The canonical data model

Record

What it represents

Trader

The individual user and their preferences

Account

One live, demo, evaluation or funded account

Connection

A platform/broker connection, its permissions and health

Order

An instruction to buy, sell, modify or cancel

Deal/fill

An actual execution, including partial fills

Position

The exposure reported by the platform

Trade episode

A journal-level grouping of related exposure and decisions

Trade plan

The trader's original thesis and planned risk

Event timeline

Entries, additions, reductions, stop changes and exits

Review

The trader's post-trade assessment and lessons

This distinction is essential. An order, a fill, a position and a journal episode are related, but they are not the same thing. The existing blueprint specifically identifies this distinction as a foundational design requirement.

Trade_Journal_App_Research_and_Implementation_Blueprint-1.pdf

How a trade should flow through the system

  1. Connect and verify. The trader authorises the connection and selects the exact account to monitor.

  2. Import account history. Fetch available historical orders, fills, positions and costs, while recording the oldest available date and any data gaps.

  3. Capture new events. Receive events through a connector, or poll the source when streaming is unavailable.

  4. Store the original source event. Save the event and its source identifiers before acknowledging receipt. Keep a deduplication key to prevent repeated events creating duplicate trades.

  5. Normalise and reconcile. Convert platform-specific symbols, timestamps, quantities and costs into the internal schema, while preserving the original values and source.

  6. Build the journal episode. Link fills, partial exits and related management events to the appropriate trade episode, with manual confirmation when matching is ambiguous.

  7. Update the user interface. Show the latest event, connection freshness, open exposure, realised results and any unresolved discrepancies.

What must happen when something goes wrong?

The system must survive disconnections, duplicated messages, delayed events, broker corrections and a terminal restart.

  • Reconnect and backfill from the last confirmed checkpoint.

  • Reprocess events safely without double-counting profit or volume.

  • Keep corrections as traceable revisions rather than silently overwriting history.

  • Distinguish confirmed values from estimates and missing data.

  • Show the last successful sync and unresolved reconciliation differences.

A connector that merely sends trade notifications is not sufficient. The goal is a reconciled trading ledger that can explain where every displayed number came from.

Trade_Journal_App_Research_and_Implementation_Blueprint-1.pdf

5. Make every trade personally journalled—with minimal friction

The journal should collect the trader's reasoning at the correct time without forcing them to complete a long questionnaire every time they execute a trade.

Before entry — plan

Instrument, direction, setup, entry zone, invalidation, stop-loss, target, intended risk, rationale, chart screenshot and checklist.

Save a timestamped, versioned plan before execution whenever possible.

During execution — timeline

Actual fill price, volume, spread/commission where available, slippage, SL/TP changes, partial closes, additions, missed entries and management notes.

Automatically capture source-observable facts; ask the trader only for missing context.

After closure — review

Net result, result in R, planned-versus-actual comparison, process adherence, optional emotions, lesson learned and one action for the next trade.

Keep the trade outcome separate from the quality of the decision.

For your own trading profile, for example, you could make Gold and Forex the default instruments, include your preferred structure/liquidity checklist and track funded-account restrictions separately for each account. These should be configurable preferences, not assumptions forced on every user.

6. Personal risk and funded-account rules engine

This module should evaluate each account independently before producing any consolidated view.

It needs to track:

  • Balance, equity and open exposure.

  • Realised and unrealised P&L, commissions, swaps and other available costs.

  • Initial risk and actual result expressed in R, with a clearly defined risk denominator.

  • Daily loss, overall drawdown and distance to any configured limit.

  • Maximum position exposure and trader-defined risk thresholds.

  • Funded-account rules such as minimum trading days, consistency rules and payout conditions—only where the user supplies or verifies the relevant rule set.

Rules must be configurable by firm, account and evaluation phase. They should include the rule's source, effective date, calculation method and any uncertainty. A generic calculation must not be presented as proof that a trader has complied with a particular firm's contract.

For the first release, this should be monitoring and alerts, not automated trade execution or a guarantee that a breach will be prevented. That boundary is consistent with the existing blueprint.

7. Personalised analytics and AI coach

Once execution records are trustworthy, the system can turn them into useful feedback.

Performance analytics

Win rate, expectancy, average win/loss, profit factor, R-multiples, drawdown, performance by strategy, session, instrument and account.

Execution quality

Compare intended and actual entry, planned and actual risk, stop management, missed rules, slippage and available execution costs.

AI review assistant

Summarise trade evidence, highlight repeated behaviours, ask targeted review questions and suggest one testable improvement.

Daily and weekly reviews

Summarise completed trades, plan adherence, risk usage, unresolved journal entries and progress on previous improvement actions.

The AI coach must explain which records support its observations. It should not infer that a trader has an edge simply because a small sample of trades was profitable, or treat a loss as proof of a bad decision.

Advanced features such as market replay, maximum adverse/favourable excursion and strategy discovery should only be activated when the required historical data is available and sufficiently reliable.

10. Acceptance criteria: how we know it works

Before launch, MofyAlly EDGE should pass measurable tests rather than simply look complete.

Area

Required test

Connection reliability

Disconnect a platform, reconnect and recover available missed history without duplicating trades.

Financial integrity

Compare imported fills, fees and account results against trusted source records.

Trade reconstruction

Correctly handle partial fills, partial exits, modifications, netting and hedging where supported.

Personalisation

Changing a trader's future template does not rewrite past plans or trades.

Multi-account isolation

One user cannot see another user's trades, screenshots or credentials.

Evidence quality

Every key figure has a source, calculation method and visible indication of missing or stale data.

Journal usability

Aim for a median quick-capture time of 20 seconds or less, validated through user testing.

TradingView events

An alert is not counted as an executed trade unless execution is independently confirmed.

Recovery and correction

Incorrect or revised source records can be traced, corrected and reflected in affected reports.

User control

Users can revoke connections and export or delete their journal data through documented workflows.

The capture-time target and data-integrity emphasis are drawn from the blueprint's proposed acceptance criteria; they must be validated in a real pilot.

The first version will focus exclusively on MetaTrader 5 (MT5) and TradingView. The goal is to make the two work together within one personalised trading workspace, while preserving the difference between a TradingView signal, an actual broker execution, and the trader's own journal notes.

3. Exact integration requirements

MT5 connector

MetaTrader's official Python package supports terminal connection, account information, active orders and positions, historical orders and deal retrieval. It requires a working MT5 terminal connection and should be tested with the specific terminal and broker configurations you intend to support.

MQL5 Reference
+1

The first connector should provide:

  • Account information and connection health.

  • Open positions and pending orders.

  • Historical orders and executed deals.

  • Entry and exit prices, volumes, timestamps, symbol and available costs.

  • SL/TP values where available, plus any changes the connector can reliably observe.

  • Periodic reconciliation and historical backfill.

  • A clear read-only permission boundary; the journal must never place or modify trades.

Technical decision: MT5's Python integration is a strong candidate for a controlled Windows-hosted connector. If you need a collector running inside the terminal itself, evaluate an observation-only MQL5 Expert Advisor instead. Choose the approach after a short proof-of-concept, not before testing connectivity, hosting and recovery.

TradingView connector

TradingView's official webhook documentation supports sending an HTTP POST request to an external endpoint when a configured alert triggers. The endpoint must respond quickly; TradingView documents a three-second processing limit and warns that webhook delivery can occasionally fail.

TradingView

The first integration should:

  • Accept alerts over HTTPS with strict payload validation.

  • Assign each received alert an internal event ID and record its timestamp.

  • Store the symbol, timeframe, alert name, strategy identifier and relevant message fields.

  • Reject malformed messages and prevent duplicate processing.

  • Return quickly, then process and match the alert asynchronously.

  • Display alert delivery status and any known gaps.

  • Never include broker passwords or other credentials in the alert payload.

For richer chart context, begin with user-supplied screenshots or chart links. Automatic extraction of arbitrary chart images or private TradingView chart state should not be assumed to be available through webhooks.

4. How the two platforms will work together

This is the most important workflow to get right.

TradingView

A configured alert fires for a trading setup

MofyAlly EDGE alert inbox

Save the signal, timestamp, symbol, timeframe and strategy context

MT5 execution capture

Import the actual deal and associate it with the relevant account and trade

Unified journal episode

Signal → planned thesis → confirmed execution → management → closure → review

If a TradingView alert fires but no MT5 execution follows, it remains a signal-only record. If an MT5 trade occurs without a matching alert, it is still captured and can be journalled as an unplanned or manually planned trade.

The matching engine should use account, instrument, direction, timing and volume as candidate clues. It should request confirmation if multiple trades or alerts could match; it must not automatically merge unrelated activity.

5. First-release dashboard

The initial dashboard should focus on six areas:

Overview

Accounts, equity, realised P&L, open exposure and connection status.

Live trades

Open positions, recent executions and event timeline.

TradingView alerts

Incoming signals, matching status and missed or unlinked events.

Trade journal

Plans, notes, screenshots, strategy tags and reviews.

Risk centre

Personal risk limits, daily results and configured account rules.

Performance

Win rate, expectancy, R-multiples, drawdown and strategy breakdowns.

Authentication · Validation · Permissions · Business logic · Integration services · Analytics

PostgreSQL

Users, accounts, trades, plans, events, reviews, rules and analytics inputs

Object storage

Chart screenshots, attachments and exported reports

Connector services, background workers and reconciliation

MT5 Connector

Accounts · Orders · Deals · Positions · History

TradingView Connector

Alerts · Symbols · Timeframes · Signal payloads

How the data moves

  1. The user enters information in a frontend form or interacts with a feature.

  2. The frontend sends an authenticated request to the FastAPI backend.

  3. The backend checks the input, validates permissions, applies business rules and writes the data to PostgreSQL.

  4. The backend returns the saved record to the frontend.

  5. The frontend updates the relevant table, dashboard, chart or status indicator.

  6. If MT5 or TradingView sends new information, the backend processes the incoming event, stores it, reconciles it with existing records and refreshes the relevant frontend views.

Core rule: the frontend must not connect directly to PostgreSQL or contain database credentials. The backend controls access to all application data.

2. Design the database around the application's data points

Use one PostgreSQL database with separate, logically organised tables rather than a separate physical database for every feature. This keeps the data connected, supports reliable calculations and allows the backend to retrieve related information efficiently.

For example, a trade's record can be linked to its user, account, original plan, MT5 orders and deals, TradingView alerts, screenshots, risk rules and review.

The following is the initial data model. Each table has a defined responsibility and links to the other relevant tables.

3. Map the relationships between the database tables

The tables must be connected through primary keys and foreign keys. This is what allows the application to answer questions such as:

  • Which MT5 account did this trade come from?

  • Which TradingView alert may have led to this execution?

  • What was the user's original plan before the trade began?

  • Which risk settings applied to this account at that time?

  • What did the user learn from the trade?

  • Which dashboard statistics must change after a new deal is imported?

Core relationship map

Important design detail: MT5 orders, deals and positions are separate records. One order can result in multiple deals, and one position can have multiple entry or exit events. Do not force them into one database row.

A trades record should act as the application's journal episode: the record the user sees and reviews as one trading idea or trade lifecycle. Its relationship to actual broker positions must accommodate the broker's account mode and partial executions. The backend should preserve the original MT5 identifiers so that reconciliation remains possible.

Essential fields and constraints

Every user-owned table should normally include:

  • id — unique internal identifier, usually a UUID.

  • user_id — owner or tenant reference where appropriate.

  • created_at and updated_at — timestamps.

  • source — where the record originated, such as user, mt5, or tradingview, where relevant.

  • metadata — optional structured supplemental data, not a substitute for core columns.

For imported MT5 records, store the external identifiers and enforce uniqueness within the correct account and source. For example, the combination of an account and an MT5 deal ticket should not be imported twice.

Use database constraints for required fields, unique external identifiers, valid enumerations and referential integrity. Store timestamps consistently in UTC and convert them to the user's preferred timezone for display.

4. Connect every feature to its backend service and database

Each feature needs a complete path: frontend component → API endpoint → backend service → database operation → response → frontend update.

A. Dashboard

Data source: trades, MT5 deals, account snapshots, risk profiles, alert status.

  • API: GET /api/v1/dashboard/summary

  • API: GET /api/v1/dashboard/equity-curve

  • API: GET /api/v1/dashboard/recent-trades

  • Backend calculates the requested statistics from validated source data and returns a consistent response.

B. Trade Journal

Data source: trades, MT5 orders/deals, trade events, tags, reviews and screenshots.

  • API: GET /api/v1/trades

  • API: GET /api/v1/trades/{trade_id}

  • API: POST /api/v1/trades

  • API: PATCH /api/v1/trades/{trade_id}

  • API: POST /api/v1/trades/{trade_id}/reviews

  • Support filtering, pagination, editing permitted journal fields and viewing the complete event timeline.

C. Trade Planning

Data source: trade plans, plan versions, risk profiles and tags.

  • API: GET /api/v1/plans

  • API: POST /api/v1/plans

  • API: PATCH /api/v1/plans/{plan_id}

  • API: POST /api/v1/plans/{plan_id}/versions

  • User input saves the original thesis, entry zone, stop-loss, targets and setup. Subsequent changes must preserve the previous plan version.

D. MT5 Accounts

Data source: trading accounts, account connections, snapshots, orders, deals, positions and sync runs.

  • API: GET /api/v1/accounts

  • API: POST /api/v1/accounts

  • API: GET /api/v1/accounts/{account_id}/connection

  • API: POST /api/v1/accounts/{account_id}/sync

  • API: GET /api/v1/accounts/{account_id}/history

  • Connector status, last sync, stale data and reconciliation errors must be visible to the user.

E. TradingView Alerts

Data source: TradingView alerts, alert-processing records and trade links.

  • API: POST /api/v1/webhooks/tradingview

  • API: GET /api/v1/alerts

  • API: POST /api/v1/alerts/{alert_id}/match

  • API: POST /api/v1/alerts/{alert_id}/dismiss

  • An incoming alert is recorded as an alert first. It must not automatically be treated as a completed trade.

F. Risk Management

Data source: risk profiles, account rule sets, trades, deals and account snapshots.

  • API: GET /api/v1/risk/profiles

  • API: PUT /api/v1/accounts/{account_id}/risk-profile

  • API: GET /api/v1/risk/status

  • API: GET /api/v1/risk/violations

  • The backend calculates configured limits and returns warnings. Each account can have its own risk settings and evaluation rules.

G. Analytics and Reports

Data source: closed trade episodes, deals, costs, tags, plans and reviews.

  • API: GET /api/v1/analytics/performance

  • API: GET /api/v1/analytics/by-strategy

  • API: GET /api/v1/analytics/by-session

  • API: GET /api/v1/analytics/risk

  • All charts and KPIs must use server-derived, consistently defined calculations rather than separate formulas scattered across frontend components.

H. Profile and Settings

Data source: users, preferences, trader profiles, account settings and notification preferences.

  • API: GET /api/v1/me

  • API: PATCH /api/v1/me

  • API: GET /api/v1/preferences

  • API: PATCH /api/v1/preferences

  • Saving a preference should update the stored value and the relevant UI. Timezone, display currency, theme and alert preferences should not require editing code.

These endpoints are a proposed API contract, not existing routes. Their request and response schemas must be defined and implemented consistently before the frontend depends on them.

5. How to connect the frontend to the backend

For MofyAlly EDGE™, use Next.js + TypeScript for the frontend, FastAPI for the backend, and PostgreSQL for persistent data.

The frontend should have a dedicated API client and a consistent data-fetching strategy. Individual pages should not invent their own backend URLs, authentication logic or calculation rules.

Recommended frontend structure

Plain text
frontend/ ├── app/ │ ├── (auth)/ │ │ ├── login/ │ │ └── register/ │ ├── (dashboard)/ │ │ ├── dashboard/ │ │ ├── journal/ │ │ ├── plans/ │ │ ├── accounts/ │ │ ├── alerts/ │ │ ├── risk/ │ │ ├── analytics/ │ │ └── settings/ │ └── layout.tsx ├── components/ │ ├── forms/ │ ├── tables/ │ ├── charts/ │ ├── dashboard/ │ └── status/ ├── features/ │ ├── trades/ │ ├── plans/ │ ├── accounts/ │ ├── alerts/ │ ├── risk/ │ └── analytics/ ├── lib/ │ ├── api-client.ts │ ├── auth.ts │ ├── query-client.ts │ └── validation.ts └── types/ ├── trade.ts ├── plan.ts ├── account.ts └── analytics.ts

Each feature owns its interface components, API functions, input validation schemas and TypeScript types. Shared components such as tables, modals, date filters and loading states can be reused.

The complete user-input cycle

Consider a user creating a new trade plan.

The frontend should not show “Saved successfully” before the backend confirms the write. If saving fails, the form should preserve the user's input and explain how to correct the problem.

Example: a shared API client

TypeScript
// lib/api-client.ts

const API_BASE_URL = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL;

export async function apiRequest<T>(
  path: string,
  options: RequestInit = {},
): Promise<T> {
  if (!API_BASE_URL) {
    throw new Error("API base URL is not configured.");
  }

  const response = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}${path}`, {
    ...options,
    credentials: "include",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      ...options.headers,
    },
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const message = await response.text();
    throw new Error(message || `Request failed: ${response.status}`);
  }

  if (response.status === 204) {
    return undefined as T;
  }

  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}

This is a starting example. Production authentication must include the agreed session or token strategy, CSRF protections where applicable, safe error parsing and consistent handling of expired sessions. Do not assume a session cookie exists until the authentication backend has implemented it.

Example: saving a trade plan

TypeScript
// features/plans/api.ts

import { apiRequest } from "@/lib/api-client";

export interface CreateTradePlan {
  symbol: string;
  direction: "BUY" | "SELL";
  timeframe: string;
  entryPrice: number;
  stopLoss: number;
  takeProfit: number;
  setup: string;
  thesis: string;
}

export interface TradePlan {
  id: string;
  symbol: string;
  direction: "BUY" | "SELL";
  status: string;
  createdAt: string;
}

export function createTradePlan(
  input: CreateTradePlan,
): Promise<TradePlan> {
  return apiRequest<TradePlan>("/api/v1/plans", {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify(input),
  });
}

A React form calls createTradePlan(input) when submitted. After success, it updates the plan list or invalidates the relevant cached query. The backend independently validates the payload; frontend validation alone is never sufficient.

Recommended addition: use TanStack Query (React Query) to manage server data, loading states, caching, retries and refetching. Use React Hook Form and Zod for consistent form handling and client-side validation. The backend remains the authority for data validation and business rules.

6. Make every feature dynamic, not hardcoded

A dynamic feature responds to saved user data, external events and backend calculations. A page displaying a chart is not truly connected just because it has a chart component.

Use this implementation standard for every feature:

Requirement

Expected behaviour

Load

Fetch the current user's records from the backend

Create

Validate and save a new record

Read

Retrieve a record by its authorised identifier

Update

Save permitted changes and return the updated record

Delete or archive

Apply the defined retention and audit rules

Search and filter

Send filters to the backend and return matching records

Pagination

Retrieve manageable pages of records

Loading state

Show progress while data is being fetched

Empty state

Explain that no records exist and offer the next useful action

Error state

Show a useful error and allow a safe retry

Freshness

Show when external data was last synchronised

Live refresh

Update views when relevant new events arrive

Permissions

Prevent users from accessing another user's records

Not every record should have unrestricted CRUD operations. For example, an imported MT5 deal is broker-originated evidence and should not be editable like a personal journal note. Corrections should be represented through a controlled process, preserving the original source record.

What should happen when user input changes?

Suppose the user changes their default timezone from UTC+3 to UTC.

  1. The settings form submits the new preference.

  2. FastAPI validates and saves it to user_preferences.

  3. The frontend receives the confirmed preference.

  4. Date and time displays use the new timezone.

  5. The underlying event timestamps remain unchanged in UTC.

  6. Reports and exports use the user's selected display timezone, while preserving the actual event time.

The same principle applies to trading strategies, risk limits, dashboard filters, alert preferences, journal tags and review templates.

Build a reusable feature pattern

Every feature should have the following components:

  • UI: forms, tables, charts and status displays.

  • Types: request and response definitions.

  • API client: functions for communicating with the backend.

  • Validation: client-side and backend validation.

  • Service: business logic in FastAPI.

  • Database model: tables, constraints and relationships.

  • Tests: validation, permissions, database behaviour and end-to-end flow.

This standard prevents the dashboard, journal and analytics modules from becoming disconnected implementations of the same data.

7. Connect MT5 and TradingView to the same trading record

This is one of the most important architectural decisions in the entire platform.

The two integrations supply different types of evidence:

  • MT5: broker-side account state, orders, deals, positions and available execution information.

  • TradingView: alerts, chart-related context, symbols, timeframes and signal payloads.

They should feed a common event-processing pipeline, but their records must retain their original sources.

Example of the matching process

A user creates a plan to sell XAUUSD. TradingView subsequently sends a sell alert. MT5 then records a sell execution.

The backend should:

  1. Save the plan with its creation timestamp and version.

  2. Record the TradingView alert with its original payload and receipt timestamp.

  3. Import the MT5 order and deal using their original identifiers.

  4. Compare account, symbol, direction, timestamps and other available matching attributes.

  5. Link the records only when the match is sufficiently reliable.

  6. Send ambiguous matches to a review queue.

  7. Update the journal's event timeline and the appropriate analytics once the underlying records have been reconciled.

A TradingView alert must not be counted as a filled order. An MT5 deal must not be counted twice because it was imported through a second synchronisation run.

How to make the integrations reliable

  • Use unique idempotency keys for incoming events.

  • Keep a durable record of received events and processing status.

  • Track sync cursors and import overlapping time windows safely.

  • Reconcile the broker's current state with imported history.

  • Handle partial fills, partial closes, corrections and reconnects.

  • Show stale connections and data gaps to the user.

  • Process incoming webhooks quickly, then perform heavier work asynchronously.

  • Never silently delete an original broker event when a correction is detected.

For the first release, make MT5 ingestion read-only. TradingView webhooks should be treated as alert inputs, not as proof of execution or as a mechanism for placing trades.

8. Organise the FastAPI backend properly

The backend should be modular, with each feature having a clear responsibility. Avoid placing all API routes, SQL queries, connector code and business rules into one large Python file.

Recommended backend directory structure

Plain text
backend/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py │ ├── core/ │ │ ├── config.py │ │ ├── security.py │ │ ├── permissions.py │ │ └── logging.py │ ├── api/ │ │ └── v1/ │ │ ├── auth.py │ │ ├── users.py │ │ ├── accounts.py │ │ ├── plans.py │ │ ├── trades.py │ │ ├── alerts.py │ │ ├── risk.py │ │ └── analytics.py │ ├── models/ │ │ ├── user.py │ │ ├── account.py │ │ ├── trade.py │ │ ├── plan.py │ │ ├── alert.py │ │ └── review.py │ ├── schemas/ │ │ ├── user.py │ │ ├── account.py │ │ ├── trade.py │ │ └── plan.py │ ├── services/ │ │ ├── trade_service.py │ │ ├── plan_service.py │ │ ├── risk_service.py │ │ ├── analytics_service.py │ │ └── matching_service.py │ ├── integrations/ │ │ ├── mt5/ │ │ └── tradingview/ │ ├── repositories/ │ │ ├── trade_repository.py │ │ ├── account_repository.py │ │ └── plan_repository.py │ ├── workers/ │ │ ├── sync_worker.py │ │ └── event_worker.py │ └── tests/ ├── migrations/ ├── alembic.ini ├── requirements.txt └── .env.example

What each layer does

Layer

Responsibility

api/

Receives HTTP requests and returns HTTP responses

schemas/

Validates request and response structures

models/

Defines database tables and relationships

services/

Implements business rules and calculations

repositories/

Encapsulates database queries and persistence

integrations/

Communicates with MT5 and receives TradingView webhooks

workers/

Handles background imports, retries and reconciliation

core/

Handles configuration, authentication and shared security

migrations/

Records controlled changes to the database schema

tests/

Verifies correctness, permissions and integrations

Use SQLAlchemy for database access and Alembic for database migrations. A migration should explicitly create or modify the necessary tables, indexes, constraints and relationships, so the schema can be deployed consistently between development, staging and production.

9. Data flow: from form submission to database and back

A typical FastAPI endpoint should not simply write arbitrary frontend data to a database. It should authenticate the user, validate the payload, enforce permissions, call the service layer and return a defined response.

For example, the trade-plan creation flow is:

Python

# Illustrative FastAPI pattern.
# The referenced schemas and service must be implemented.

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, status
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

router = APIRouter(prefix="/plans", tags=["Trade Plans"])


@router.post("", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
async def create_plan(
payload: "TradePlanCreate",
current_user=Depends(get_current_user),
db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
):
plan = await plan_service.create_plan(
db=db,
user_id=current_user.id,
payload=payload,
)

return plan

The important design decision is that plan_service.create_plan() owns the business process. It should validate trading-specific conditions, write the plan and initial version consistently, and ensure the plan belongs to the authenticated user.

This is illustrative, not a complete executable endpoint: authentication dependencies, database sessions, schemas, service implementation and response models must also be defined.

10. Make the database reliable and secure

Because this platform contains trading history, account information and potentially sensitive financial records, security must be part of the initial architecture.

Essential controls

  • User isolation: every user-owned query must be scoped to the authenticated user. Never trust a user_id supplied by the frontend as proof of ownership.

  • Authentication: use a secure session or token design, with appropriate password hashing, session expiry, revocation and account recovery.

  • Database security: use parameterised queries, least-privilege database accounts, encrypted connections and managed secrets.

  • Connection credentials: never expose MT5 credentials, webhook secrets, API keys or database credentials in frontend code, logs or URLs.

  • Webhook validation: authenticate TradingView webhook requests using a documented secure design, validate the payload, apply rate limits and reject malformed events.

  • Auditability: record important changes to plans, settings, risk limits, connections and journal records.

  • Backups: automate backups and test actual restoration.

  • Data rights: support authorised exports, account disconnection and deletion according to the product's retention policy.

  • Concurrent updates: use database transactions and suitable constraints so simultaneous imports do not produce duplicates or inconsistent financial totals.

For live MT5 access, the connector requires a suitable running MT5 terminal environment. It should be isolated from the public web server and communicate with the backend through authenticated internal interfaces. Do not expose a desktop terminal or its credentials directly to the browser.

11. Make dashboard data update automatically

A connected app should reflect new data without forcing users to refresh every page manually.

Use three complementary methods:

1. Scheduled synchronisation

The MT5 worker periodically imports new account state, orders and deals. It also runs reconciliation and records sync health.

2. Event-driven updates

TradingView webhooks and completed import jobs produce events that can trigger relevant data refreshes.

3. WebSocket or server-sent events

The backend notifies connected browser sessions when important records change. The frontend then refreshes affected queries.

These methods complement each other. A browser notification is not a substitute for durable database storage, and a real-time connection should recover gracefully after disconnection.

For example, when an MT5 deal is imported, the backend should persist and reconcile it first, then notify the frontend. The journal, account summary and performance charts can refresh from the authoritative API response.

12. Build the project in the correct order

Do not build every screen first and attempt to connect everything at the end. Establish a working vertical slice, from the database to the interface, and repeat that pattern for each feature.

01

Foundation and authentication

Phase 1

Create the repository, environment configuration, FastAPI application, PostgreSQL database, migrations, authentication, user isolation and API conventions.

02

Core user data and trade planning

Phase 2

Build profiles, preferences, accounts, plans, plan versions, journal forms and complete create/read/update flows. Verify that data persists after logout and login.

03

MT5 ingestion

Phase 3

Prove account connectivity, history import, open-position snapshots, deal deduplication, reconnection and reconciliation. Populate the journal from actual imported data.

04

TradingView integration

Phase 4

Implement secure webhook ingestion, payload validation, event storage, alert history, delivery/processing status and user-controlled matching.

05

Risk, reviews and analytics

Phase 5

Implement validated calculations, configurable risk profiles, funded-account rules, trade reviews, filters, charts and export.

06

Live updates, testing and production

Phase 6

Add event notifications, retry handling, monitoring, backup restoration tests, permission tests, performance checks and a controlled pilot.

The duration of each phase should be set after the MT5 connection method, deployment environment and TradingView webhook requirements are proven. Do not assume the earlier 16-week roadmap is guaranteed.

13. Definition of done: how to know the system is truly connected

Before declaring a feature complete, verify all of the following:

My recommendation for MofyAlly EDGE™

Start by implementing one complete vertical slice:

  1. The user registers and configures a profile.

  2. The user creates an MT5 account record and a trade plan.

  3. The MT5 connector imports real account history into the database.

  4. TradingView sends an alert that is stored independently.

  5. The backend links the alert, plan and execution only when appropriate.

  6. The journal displays the complete timeline.

  7. The dashboard recalculates its statistics from the verified data.

Once this works end to end, use the same architecture for reviews, risk management, analytics and every subsequent feature.

That approach will give MofyAlly EDGE™ a maintainable foundation in which every feature has a defined data source, every user input has a persistence path, every integration has an explicit connection contract, and every displayed metric can be traced back to its underlying records.
